contents.html: This paper presents a framework for evaluating conformance of a protocol implementation to the Security Protocol at layer 4 (SP4) standard. SP4 is one element of the Secure Data Network System (SDNS) architecture, used to provide security services at the Transport layer of the Open System Interconnection (OSI) reference model. SP4 also forms the basis of the ISO standard for the OSI Transport Layer Security Protocol (TLSP). Therefore, with few exceptions, the findings of the paper are applicable to TLSP. The paper explores the relationship between conformance assessment, interoperability assessment, and security evaluation of security protocols. The OSI conformance testing methodology and framework is reviewed, and a strategy is given for applying this methodology to SP4 implementations.
contents.html_ja: この論文は、プロトコルの実装が、レイヤ 4 のセキュリティプロトコル（SP4）標準に適合しているかどうかを評価するための枠組みを示します。SP4 は、Secure Data Network System（SDNS）アーキテクチャの要素の 1 つで、開放型システム間相互接続（OSI）参照モデルのトランスポート層でセキュリティサービスを提供するために使われます。SP4 は、OSI トランスポート層セキュリティプロトコル（TLSP）の ISO 標準の基礎にもなっています。そのため、少数の例外を除き、この論文の知見は TLSP にも適用できます。この論文は、セキュリティプロトコルの適合性評価、相互運用性評価、セキュリティ評価の関係を検討します。OSI の適合性試験の方法論と枠組みを概観し、この方法論を SP4 の実装に適用するための戦略を示します。

contents.html: The Secure Data Network System (SDNS) [5] program began in August of 1986 through the sponsorship of the National Security Agency (NSA). The goal of the program is to establish a communications architecture and protocols for protecting both unclassified and classified computer networks, within an internationally recognized framework. Security Protocol 4 (SP4) [3,4] is one element of the SDNS, designed to provide security services at layer 4, the Transport layer, of the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) reference model for Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) [1].
contents.html_ja: Secure Data Network System（SDNS）[5] プログラムは、国家安全保障局（NSA）の後援により、1986 年 8 月に開始されました。このプログラムの目標は、国際的に認められた枠組みの中で、非機密と機密の両方のコンピュータネットワークを保護するための通信アーキテクチャとプロトコルを確立することです。Security Protocol 4（SP4）[3,4] は SDNS の要素の 1 つで、国際標準化機構（ISO）の開放型システム間相互接続（OSI）参照モデル [1] のレイヤ 4、すなわちトランスポート層で、セキュリティサービスを提供するよう設計されています。

contents.html: The SP4 standard builds upon the services of either the connectionless or connection oriented Transport layer protocol. It should be viewed as an extension to those protocol standards, rather than as an independent layer protocol. In the OSI architecture, the Transport layer has the sole responsibility to provide reliable end-to-end communications between peer end-systems. SP4 services, therefore, nicely complement those provided by Transport protocols. SP4 functionality is situated near the bottom of the Transport layer and consists of a simple encapsulation/decapsulation mechanism that protects Transport protocol data units within a cryptographically secure envelope. SP4 extends the OSI Transport connectionless and connection oriented services to provide or support the following security services defined in the OSI Security Architecture addendum to the reference model [2]:
contents.html_ja: SP4 標準は、コネクションレス型またはコネクション指向型のいずれかのトランスポート層プロトコルのサービスの上に成り立っています。SP4 は、独立した層のプロトコルとしてではなく、それらのプロトコル標準の拡張として捉えるべきです。OSI アーキテクチャでは、トランスポート層は、対等なエンドシステム間で信頼できるエンドツーエンドの通信を提供する責任だけを負っています。したがって、SP4 のサービスは、トランスポートプロトコルが提供するサービスをうまく補完します。SP4 の機能は、トランスポート層の下部付近に位置し、トランスポートプロトコルデータユニットを暗号によって保護された封筒の中に入れて守る、単純なカプセル化・脱カプセル化の仕組みで構成されています。SP4 は、OSI のトランスポートのコネクションレス型およびコネクション指向型のサービスを拡張し、参照モデルへの OSI セキュリティアーキテクチャの追補 [2] で定義された次のセキュリティサービスを提供または支援します。

contents.html: The SP4 standard identifies other security functions on which it depends. These functions include key management, security management, and cryptography. Key management is needed to establish and maintain keying material used by SP4; security management is needed for event reporting and auditing; and cryptography (i.e., employment of specific cryptographic algorithms) is needed to support Data Integrity, Data Confidentiality, and Authentication services. These functions are normally collocated in an end-system, with an SP4 entity.
contents.html_ja: SP4 標準は、SP4 が依存するほかのセキュリティ機能を明らかにしています。これらの機能には、鍵管理、セキュリティ管理、暗号が含まれます。鍵管理は、SP4 が使う鍵素材を確立し維持するために必要です。セキュリティ管理は、イベントの報告と監査のために必要です。暗号（すなわち特定の暗号アルゴリズムの使用）は、データの完全性、データの機密性、認証のサービスを支えるために必要です。これらの機能は通常、SP4 エンティティとともにエンドシステム内に配置されます。

contents.html: This paper investigates the conformance assessment of an SP4 implementation and the implications of such a procedure. Since SP4 is compliant with the OSI reference model and security architecture, emphasis is placed on the OSI conformance testing methodology [9]. Two other related assessment methods, interoperability assessment and security evaluation, are also reviewed. Like conformance assessment, both are concerned with the correctness of an implementation, albeit from different perspectives.
contents.html_ja: この論文は、SP4 の実装の適合性評価と、そのような手順の含意を調査します。SP4 は OSI 参照モデルとセキュリティアーキテクチャに準拠しているため、OSI の適合性試験の方法論 [9] に重点を置いています。関連する 2 つの評価方法、相互運用性評価とセキュリティ評価についても概観します。この 2 つは、適合性評価と同様に、実装の正しさに関わるものですが、視点が異なります。

contents.html: An implicit assumption made throughout this paper is that for an SP4 implementation to be trustworthy, the SP4 layer protocol entity must be part of the Trusted Computing Base (TCB) [15] for a distributed system. Figure 1 illustrates this view of SP4. A TCB refers to the combination of protection mechanisms within a computer system responsible for enforcing a security policy. In a distributed network environment, this is referred to as a Network Trusted Computing Base (NTCB) [13].

contents.html: Conformance assessment of OSI protocols is defined in a multi-part standard [9] that provides the basic framework and methodology for conformance testing. The scope of the standard ranges from abstract test suite specification and executable test derivation to the conformance assessment process, and includes test methods and a formal notation for describing test cases. The assessment procedure has two distinct parts: a static conformance review of the Protocol Implementation Conformance Statement (PICS) and dynamic conformance testing of the implementation.
contents.html_ja: OSI プロトコルの適合性評価は、適合性試験の基本的な枠組みと方法論を示す複数部からなる標準 [9] で定義されています。この標準の範囲は、抽象試験スイートの仕様と実行可能な試験の導出から、適合性評価プロセスまで及び、試験方法と、試験ケースを記述するための形式的な表記を含みます。評価手順には 2 つの別個の部分があります。Protocol Implementation Conformance Statement（PICS）の静的な適合性レビューと、実装の動的な適合性試験です。

contents.html: The PICS defines, in a tabular form, the range of functionality (i.e., capabilities and options) afforded by an implementation. Product manufacturers are expected to provide PICS for their implementations according to the PICS proforma established by standardization groups for an OSI protocol. By reviewing the PICS, a determination can be made of whether or not the functionality provided by a product meets the conformance requirements. The PICS also can be used as a guide for selecting appropriate test cases against which to assess the conformance claims of an implementation. The methodology also requires a Protocol Implementation Extra Information for Testing (PIXIT) to identify additional information about an implementation to facilitate testing, such as address values, timers, and parameter settings.
contents.html_ja: PICS は、実装が提供する機能の範囲（すなわち能力とオプション）を、表形式で定義します。製品の製造者は、OSI プロトコルについて標準化グループが定めた PICS の様式に従って、自らの実装の PICS を提供することが求められます。PICS をレビューすることで、製品が提供する機能が適合性要件を満たしているかどうかを判断できます。PICS は、実装の適合性の主張を評価する際の、適切な試験ケースを選択するための指針としても使えます。この方法論は、試験を円滑にするために、アドレス値、タイマー、パラメータ設定など、実装に関する追加情報を特定する Protocol Implementation Extra Information for Testing（PIXIT）も必要とします。

contents.html: Conformance testing for OSI is the process of verifying that the external behavior of an implemented data communications protocol agrees with the requirements specified in the defining standard. The OSI conformance testing methodology relies on a black box testing approach. That is, the internals of the box, or in this situation the protocol implementation under test, are unexaminable and unknown. How the protocol functionality is implemented is not part of the methodology. Instead, emphasis is placed on external behavior.
contents.html_ja: OSI の適合性試験は、実装されたデータ通信プロトコルの外部から見た振る舞いが、それを定義する標準に定められた要件に合致していることを検証するプロセスです。OSI の適合性試験の方法論は、ブラックボックス試験のアプローチに依拠しています。つまり、箱の内部、この場合は試験対象のプロトコルの実装は、調べることができず、未知のままです。プロトコルの機能がどのように実装されているかは、この方法論の対象ではありません。代わりに、外部から見た振る舞いに重点が置かれます。

contents.html: The external behavior of an OSI protocol implementation is observable through the protocol data units (PDUs) exchanged with a test system, and is the foundation for the design of test scenarios. OSI conformance test scenarios contain negative as well as positive tests. That is, test scenarios include test cases involving the use of invalid PDUs and otherwise inappropriate PDU behavior. Conformance testing can determine whether PDUs are correctly exchanged, services are correctly provided, options are correctly treated, errors are correctly handled, and events are correctly reported.
contents.html_ja: OSI プロトコルの実装の外部から見た振る舞いは、試験システムとやり取りするプロトコルデータユニット（PDU）を通じて観察でき、試験シナリオの設計の基礎となります。OSI の適合性試験シナリオには、肯定的な試験だけでなく否定的な試験も含まれます。つまり、試験シナリオには、無効な PDU の使用や、その他の不適切な PDU の振る舞いを伴う試験ケースが含まれます。適合性試験によって、PDU が正しく交換されているか、サービスが正しく提供されているか、オプションが正しく扱われているか、エラーが正しく処理されているか、イベントが正しく報告されているかを判断できます。

contents.html: While conformance testing increases the probability that different implementations of a set of selected protocols will interwork properly, it is no guarantee of full interoperability, given the typically large number of protocol options and unconstrained parameters. Supplementary interoperability assessment is also required.
contents.html_ja: 適合性試験は、選択された一連のプロトコルの異なる実装が正しく相互動作する確率を高めますが、一般にプロトコルのオプションが多数あり、パラメータが制約されていないことを考えると、完全な相互運用性を保証するものではありません。補足的な相互運用性評価も必要です。

contents.html: Similar to conformance assessment, the focus of interoperability assessment is testing. Interoperability testing is concerned with the end-to-end operation of one or more OSI implementations, exercising all services with various semantic values, and checking rendition and expected behavior. For example, in the case of messaging systems, the data content must be correctly relayed across several end-systems and correctly rendered to the recipients. Moreover, the distribution and handling within the end-system must behave as expected.
contents.html_ja: 適合性評価と同様に、相互運用性評価では試験に重点が置かれます。相互運用性試験では、1 つ以上の OSI 実装のエンドツーエンドの動作を対象に、さまざまな意味内容の値を用いてすべてのサービスを実行し、表示内容と期待される振る舞いを確認します。たとえば、メッセージングシステムの場合、データの内容は、複数のエンドシステムを経由して正しく中継され、受信者に正しく表示されなければなりません。さらに、エンドシステム内での配布と処理も、期待どおりに振る舞わなければなりません。

contents.html: Although interoperability testing also uses a black box approach, it contrasts from conformance testing in several ways. Perhaps the most striking is the change from a test environment involving a validated test system and instrumented implementation, to an operational environment involving many different implementations as counterparts to the testing. Another significant difference is that the OSI conformance testing methodology is concerned primarily with evaluating a single layer or small group of layers, while interoperability testing involves the entire seven layer stack or, in the case of intermediate systems, the lower-level three-layer stack. Interoperability testing also emphasizes positive as opposed to negative testing, in contrast to conformance testing.
contents.html_ja: 相互運用性試験もブラックボックスのアプローチを使いますが、適合性試験とはいくつかの点で対照的です。おそらく最も顕著なのは、検証済みの試験システムと計装された実装を伴う試験環境から、試験の相手として多くの異なる実装が関わる運用環境へと変わることです。もう 1 つの大きな違いは、OSI の適合性試験の方法論が主に単一の層または少数の層の集まりを評価することに関わっているのに対し、相互運用性試験は 7 層のスタック全体、または中継システムの場合は下位 3 層のスタックを対象とすることです。相互運用性試験は、適合性試験とは対照的に、否定的な試験ではなく肯定的な試験を重視する点も特徴です。

contents.html: Interoperability testing alone is not a substitute for conformance testing. There always exists the danger of obtaining implementations that are interoperable with each other, but not necessarily conformant to the protocol standard. Because of the emphasis on positive testing, there is also the possibility that interoperability tests would not uncover some types of errors. Therefore, both types of testing are needed to preclude isolated islands of interoperable but non-conformant implementations.
contents.html_ja: 相互運用性試験だけでは、適合性試験の代わりにはなりません。互いに相互運用できるものの、プロトコル標準に適合しているとは限らない実装が得られる危険が常にあります。肯定的な試験が重視されるため、相互運用性試験で、ある種の誤りが見つからない可能性もあります。したがって、相互運用はできるが適合していない実装の孤立した島ができることを防ぐために、両方の種類の試験が必要です。

contents.html: At present, interoperability testing is not the subject of international standardization, due to a lack of broad consensus of a methodology and framework. Most interoperability testing is conducted on an ad hoc basis, to meet the demands of a particular situation. Implementations intended for a specific management domain may be subjected to interoperability tests as part of the requirement for membership. Many commercial implementations go through such a phase prior to and during vendor demonstrations at international trade shows and conferences. As demonstration software matures into products, reasonable product interoperability becomes the norm.
contents.html_ja: 現時点では、方法論と枠組みについて広範な合意がないため、相互運用性試験は国際標準化の対象になっていません。相互運用性試験の大半は、特定の状況の要求に応えるために、アドホックに実施されています。特定の管理ドメイン向けの実装は、加入の要件の一部として、相互運用性試験を受けることがあります。多くの商用の実装は、国際的な見本市や会議での供給者のデモンストレーションの前および最中に、このような段階を経ます。デモンストレーション用のソフトウェアが製品へと成熟するにつれて、妥当な製品の相互運用性が当たり前になります。

contents.html: A security evaluation assesses products to determine the degree of trust that can be placed in them with regard to the secure processing of information. An evaluation is done without regard to the specific operational conditions and circumstances in which a product may be used (e.g., inside a shielded vault), but does take into consideration the computer system operating environment. The objective of the security evaluation is to perform a technical assessment of the trust properties. Three general security issues that must be addressed are: the confidentiality of the data, the integrity of the data and the system, and the availability of service. The goal or main requirement is to assure that the system behaves according to an organization’s security requirements that, in turn, reflect the defined security policy of the organization. To guarantee that this requirement is met, the security functionality of an implementation must work correctly and effectively.
contents.html_ja: セキュリティ評価は、情報の安全な処理に関して製品にどの程度の信頼を置けるかを判断するために、製品を評価するものです。評価は、製品が使われる可能性のある特定の運用条件や状況（たとえば遮へいされた保管室の中）にかかわらず行われますが、コンピュータシステムの運用環境は考慮に入れます。セキュリティ評価の目的は、信頼に関する特性の技術的な評価を行うことです。対処しなければならない一般的なセキュリティ上の課題は、データの機密性、データとシステムの完全性、サービスの可用性の 3 つです。目標、すなわち主要な要件は、システムが、組織のセキュリティ要件に従って動作することを保証することであり、そのセキュリティ要件は、組織が定めたセキュリティポリシーを反映するものです。この要件が満たされることを保証するためには、実装のセキュリティ機能が正しく効果的に動作しなければなりません。

contents.html: Evaluations of commercial products in the U.S. are carried out through the Department of Defense (DoD) Trusted Product Evaluation Program (TPEP). The TPEP evaluates systems that meet the DoD’s program objectives based on the criteria defined in the DoD TCSEC [7]. The TCSEC defines a hierarchy of classes that represent increasing levels of confidence in the trustworthiness of a computer system to protect information. The TCSEC identifies features to be evaluated, such as login, access controls, and audit; and assurances to be obtained, such as least privilege, testing, and documentation. Features are mechanisms that provide security functionality, while assurances indicate the degree of trust, and give a measure of the degree to which features work correctly and are effective.
contents.html_ja: 米国における商用製品の評価は、国防総省（DoD）の Trusted Product Evaluation Program（TPEP）を通じて実施されます。TPEP は、DoD の TCSEC [7] で定義されたクライテリアに基づいて、DoD のプログラムの目的を満たすシステムを評価します。TCSEC は、情報を保護するコンピュータシステムの信頼性に対する確信のレベルが段階的に高まることを表す、クラスの階層を定義しています。TCSEC は、ログイン、アクセス制御、監査などの評価すべき機能と、最小権限、試験、文書化などの得るべき保証を特定しています。機能はセキュリティ機能を提供するメカニズムであり、保証は信頼の度合いを示し、機能がどの程度正しく動作し効果的であるかの尺度を与えます。

contents.html: In contrast to conformance and interoperability evaluation techniques, security evaluations are limited to only the security relevant portions of the system. However, an evaluation at higher levels of assurance may be extensive, especially if one considers the attention given such areas as covert channels. Furthermore, testing is only one aspect of a security evaluation. Other aspects include ensuring that the product is produced and distributed according to appropriate controls and standards, and ensuring that well documented procedures exist for the operational use of the product. The goal of an evaluator is to gain a deep understanding of a product and how it meets stated security objectives, not merely to determine whether it passes a set of predefined tests.
contents.html_ja: 適合性評価や相互運用性評価の技法とは対照的に、セキュリティ評価は、システムのうちセキュリティに関連する部分だけに限定されます。ただし、より高い保証レベルでの評価は、特に隠れチャネルなどの領域に払われる注意を考えれば、広範囲に及ぶことがあります。さらに、試験はセキュリティ評価の 1 つの側面にすぎません。ほかの側面には、製品が適切な統制と標準に従って製造・配布されていることの確認や、製品の運用上の使用について十分に文書化された手順が存在することの確認が含まれます。評価者の目標は、あらかじめ定義された一連の試験に合格するかどうかを判断するだけではなく、製品と、それが定められたセキュリティの目的をどのように満たしているかを深く理解することです。

contents.html: TCSEC evaluations are normally carried out in parallel with product development. Features (i.e., security mechanisms) not only must be operable and correct, but also must be implemented to resist tampering and leakage. From a testing perspective, assurance is gained through testing the implementation’s security functionality and susceptibility to penetration. An evaluator has access to internal documentation and is involved in the product development cycle. Security evaluations under the TCSEC can be considered a form of white box testing, since the internals of the box can be observed and controlled, and specifications of the internal design are available for analysis. White box testing is typically more stringent than black box testing since it allows test case design to establish some measure of minimum execution coverage with respect to the structural properties of software and hardware under evaluation.
contents.html_ja: TCSEC の評価は通常、製品開発と並行して実施されます。機能（すなわちセキュリティメカニズム）は、動作可能で正しいだけでなく、改ざんと漏えいに耐えるように実装されていなければなりません。試験の観点では、保証は、実装のセキュリティ機能と、侵入への脆弱性を試験することで得られます。評価者は内部文書にアクセスでき、製品開発サイクルに関与します。TCSEC によるセキュリティ評価は、箱の内部を観察して制御でき、内部設計の仕様を分析に利用できるため、ホワイトボックス試験の一形態とみなせます。ホワイトボックス試験は、評価対象のソフトウェアとハードウェアの構造上の特性に関して、最小限の実行網羅率の何らかの尺度を確立するように試験ケースを設計できるため、通常、ブラックボックス試験よりも厳格です。

contents.html: Although concerned with the provision of security services through specific types of security mechanisms, the SP4 standard does not contain any requirements on the level of confidence in the security provided by an implementation of the protocol. That is, the SP4 standard is a functionality specification devoid of assurance requirements for the implementation and the operating environment. Therefore, an implementation may fully conform to the SP4 standard, yet be inherently insecure. For example, there are no guarantees that a system correctly implementing SP4 either employs algorithms with an appropriate strength of mechanism, or controls access to transmitted information once it resides in the system. The level of assurance provided by an SP4 implementation depends on factors outside the scope of the standard. That assurance can be gained only by evaluating the implementation according to an established set of criteria, such as the DoD Trusted Computer System Evaluation Criteria (TCSEC) [7] or Trusted Network Interpretation [15] of that criteria.
contents.html_ja: 特定の種類のセキュリティメカニズムによるセキュリティサービスの提供を扱ってはいますが、SP4 標準には、プロトコルの実装によって提供されるセキュリティに対する確信のレベルについての要件は含まれていません。つまり、SP4 標準は、実装と運用環境に対する保証要件を欠いた、機能の仕様です。したがって、実装が SP4 標準に完全に適合していても、本質的に安全でない場合があります。たとえば、SP4 を正しく実装したシステムが、適切なメカニズムの強度を持つアルゴリズムを使っていること、あるいは、送信される情報がシステム内に存在する間のアクセスを制御していることは、保証されません。SP4 の実装が提供する保証のレベルは、標準の範囲外の要因に依存します。その保証は、DoD の Trusted Computer System Evaluation Criteria（TCSEC）[7] やそのクライテリアの Trusted Network Interpretation [15] のような、確立された一連のクライテリアに従って実装を評価することによってのみ得られます。

contents.html: The SP4 standard is mechanism dependent, but algorithm independent. For example, the Data Confidentiality service is provided through an encipherment mechanism, but the underlying cryptographic algorithm is left open in the specification. Furthermore, an SP4 implementation may legitimately support only a subset of the optional elements indicated in the standard. To compensate for the openness and flexibility in the standard, implementors’ groups are expected to develop security sub-profiles for generic applications. That is, the characteristics of the required security functionality must be stipulated before an implementation can be constructed.
contents.html_ja: SP4 標準は、メカニズムに依存しますが、アルゴリズムには依存しません。たとえば、データの機密性サービスは暗号化のメカニズムによって提供されますが、基礎となる暗号アルゴリズムは仕様では特定されていません。さらに、SP4 の実装は、標準に示されたオプション要素の一部のみをサポートしても、正当と認められます。標準のこの開放性と柔軟性を補うため、実装者のグループが、汎用のアプリケーション向けにセキュリティのサブプロファイルを策定することが期待されています。つまり、実装を構築する前に、必要なセキュリティ機能の特性を規定しなければなりません。

contents.html: A security sub-profile specifies the general security objectives and operating environment assumptions, a target range of assurance, and suites of protection algorithms, in addition to the set of security features selected from those offered by the protocol. Therefore, a protection profile not only tightens the functionality specification, but also supplements it with assurance requirements. Few examples of security sub-profiles exist. Probably the best known example is that done for Message Handling Systems based on the X.400 standard [10].
contents.html_ja: セキュリティのサブプロファイルは、プロトコルが提供するもののうちから選択されたセキュリティ機能の集合に加えて、一般的なセキュリティの目的と運用環境の前提条件、保証の目標範囲、保護アルゴリズムの組を規定します。したがって、プロテクションプロファイルは、機能の仕様を厳密にするだけでなく、保証要件でそれを補います。セキュリティのサブプロファイルの例はほとんどありません。おそらく最もよく知られた例は、X.400 標準 [10] に基づくメッセージ処理システム向けに作成されたものです。

contents.html: In practice, a fully capable SP4 implementation is an implementation of a Transport protocol with embedded SP4 functionality. contents.html: Clearly, the objective and scope of the three categories of assessment are quite different. Conformance assessment is the most functionally precise, since it provides testing at the level of detail of the functional standard, on a protocol-by-protocol basis. Interoperability assessment is a bit broader since it concerns a group of layer protocols and their operational aspects, and seeks functional compatibility among many implementations. Security evaluation is somewhat orthogonal to both. In the case of SP4, it is broader in scope than conformance testing of a protocol entity, yet narrower than interoperability testing of an entire end-system. The target of a security evaluation, the trusted computing base, lies somewhere in between. Similarly, while the objective of a security evaluation goes beyond functionality and seeks adherence to assurance requirements, only the correctness and effectiveness of the implementation from a security perspective are of concern. Therefore, it is possible to successfully evaluate an SP4 implementation that lacks conformance to the standard and does not interoperate with other implementations.
contents.html_ja: 評価の 3 つの区分の目的と範囲は、明らかにかなり異なります。適合性評価は、プロトコルごとに機能標準の詳細さの水準で試験を行うため、機能的には最も正確です。相互運用性評価は、一群の層プロトコルとその運用面に関わり、多くの実装間の機能的な互換性を求めるため、やや広くなります。セキュリティ評価は、その両方に対して、ある意味で直交しています。SP4 の場合、範囲はプロトコルエンティティの適合性試験より広く、エンドシステム全体の相互運用性試験よりは狭くなります。セキュリティ評価の対象である Trusted Computing Base は、その中間のどこかにあります。同様に、セキュリティ評価の目的は、機能を超えて、保証要件への準拠を求めるものですが、関心の対象は、セキュリティの観点からの実装の正しさと有効性だけです。したがって、標準に適合しておらず、ほかの実装と相互運用もできない SP4 の実装であっても、評価を成功裏に終えられる可能性があります。

contents.html: Although OSI conformance testing does not directly address trust-related factors of an implementation, a successful conformance testing result suggests a level of assurance for the implementation. That is, contrary to the traditional view of separate conformance and security evaluations, conformance testing could be integrated into the security evaluation process and be made a part of the evaluation procedure for a distributed system that relies on a lower layer security protocol such as SP4.

contents.html: One interesting difference between conformance and security evaluations is in the structure of the processes and the roles that the organizations play in them. The security evaluation of a product is normally done through a sponsoring governmental agency, includes product development as part of the process, is conducted at a secure government facility using procedures not completely disclosed to the public, and continues until the criteria level is met or the developer gives up. A conformance evaluation on the other hand is normally initiated by the developer, is conducted after product development, is evaluated at a government accredited facility through publicly available test procedures, and renders a pass/fail verdict within a comparatively short period of time. Whereas the security evaluation process is centered around the concerns of the evaluation agency, the conformance evaluation process is oriented more toward the developer. In particular, the black box nature of conformance testing avoids disclosure of proprietary information by the developer.
contents.html_ja: 適合性評価とセキュリティ評価の興味深い違いの 1 つは、プロセスの構造と、その中で組織が果たす役割にあります。製品のセキュリティ評価は、通常、後援する政府機関のもとで行われ、製品開発をプロセスの一部として含み、完全には公開されていない手順を使って、安全な政府施設で実施され、クライテリアのレベルを満たすか、開発者が断念するまで続きます。一方、適合性評価は、通常、開発者が開始し、製品開発の後に実施され、公開されている試験手順を使って、政府が認定した施設で評価され、比較的短期間で合格・不合格の判定が下されます。セキュリティ評価のプロセスが評価機関の関心を中心にしているのに対し、適合性評価のプロセスは、より開発者に向けられています。特に、適合性試験がブラックボックスの性質を持つことで、開発者の専有情報の開示が避けられます。

contents.html: The implication of these assumptions is that an SP4 implementation must be tested indirectly, through the interface to the Transport protocol entity. The approach taken is to build upon extant testing requirements for the Government Open System Interconnection Profile (GOSIP) [12]. The abstract test method proposed for SP4 follows a coordinated single-layer embedded test method. This approach assumes that explicit test coordination procedures can be used with the Transport implementation containing and/or supporting SP4 functionality. Figure 2 illustrates this test method for SP4. The system under test must involve a Transport implementation whose normal non-security services have been successfully tested. Here the Transport protocol interface is used as the point of control and observation (PCO) for the upper tester, in lieu of an exposed SP4 interface. contents.html: Within the U.S. Federal Government, the Government OSI Profile (GOSIP) [11] is the procurement specification for agencies to use when acquiring open systems computer network products. GOSIP conformance testing procedures [12] have been established that follow the OSI conformance testing methodology. At the Transport layer, GOSIP mandates class 4 Transport for interoperability among compliant systems. The remaining classes have a less essential role in the specification, as does the connectionless Transport protocol. For this reason, and because class 4 functionality encompasses that of the other classes, only class 4 test cases are considered in the discussion that follows.
contents.html_ja: 米国連邦政府内では、Government OSI Profile（GOSIP）[11] が、各機関が開放型システムのコンピュータネットワーク製品を調達する際に使用する調達仕様です。OSI の適合性試験の方法論に従った、GOSIP の適合性試験手順 [12] が確立されています。トランスポート層では、GOSIP は、準拠するシステム間の相互運用性のために、クラス 4 のトランスポートを必須としています。残りのクラスは、コネクションレス型のトランスポートプロトコルと同様に、仕様の中での役割がそれほど重要ではありません。このため、またクラス 4 の機能がほかのクラスの機能を包含するため、以下の議論では、クラス 4 の試験ケースだけを考慮します。

contents.html: The abstract test cases for the class 4 Transport protocol fall into one of three categories of increasing complexity and functionality: basic interconnection tests, capability tests, and behavior tests. Basic interconnection tests establish a baseline capability and determine the ability of the implementation to open and close connections, and convey normal user data, and parameters. Capability tests continue to examine fully all mandatory capabilities and determine whether the implementation can convey expedited data, and more extensive amounts of normal user data. Behavior tests establish the extent to which the dynamic conformance requirements are met and examine the ability of the implementation to negotiate parameters, to be involved in more complicated exchanges, and to handle the full range of error conditions.
contents.html_ja: クラス 4 のトランスポートプロトコルの抽象試験ケースは、複雑さと機能が段階的に高まる 3 つの区分のいずれかに分類されます。基本相互接続試験、能力試験、振る舞い試験です。基本相互接続試験は、基準となる能力を確立し、実装がコネクションを開閉し、通常の利用者データとパラメータを伝達する能力を判定します。能力試験では、すべての必須能力を引き続き詳しく調べ、実装が緊急データや、より大量の通常の利用者データを伝達できるかどうかを判定します。振る舞い試験は、動的な適合性要件がどの程度満たされているかを確認し、実装がパラメータを交渉し、より複雑なやり取りに関与し、あらゆる範囲のエラー状態を処理する能力を調べます。

contents.html: GOSIP test scenarios for class 4 Transport are not capable of providing insight into an SP4 IUT, other than to establish that fundamental communications capabilities are in good order. Furthermore, the behavior tests are no longer appropriate since they do not address the specific services offered by SP4. These security services are embodied in the security encapsulation (SE) TPDU, used exclusively by the SP4 protocol. None of the error conditions associated with the SE TPDU are part of the existing behavior tests.

U.S. DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE Technology Administration National Institute of Standards and Technology Computer Systems Laboratory Gaithersburg, MD 20899
Conformance Assessment of Transport Layer Security Implementations
U.S. DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE Technology Administration National Institute of Standards and Technology Computer Systems Laboratory Gaithersburg, MD 20899
U.S. DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE Ronald H. Brown, Secretary TECHNOLOGY ADMINISTRATION Mary L Good, Linder Secretary for Technology NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF STANDARDS AND TECHNOLOGY Arati Prabhakar, Director

This paper presents a framework for evaluating conformance of a protocol implementation to the Security Protocol at layer 4 (SP4) standard. SP4 is one element of the Secure Data Network System (SDNS) architecture, used to provide security services at the Transport layer of the Open System Interconnection (OSI) reference model. SP4 also forms the basis of the ISO standard for the OSI Transport Layer Security Protocol (TLSP). Therefore, with few exceptions, the findings of the paper are applicable to TLSP. The paper explores the relationship between conformance assessment, interoperability assessment, and security evaluation of security protocols. The OSI conformance testing methodology and framework is reviewed, and a strategy is given for applying this
Keywords: OSI, Lower Layer Security Protocols, Conformance Testing, Security
3.3 Characteristics of the Means of Testing
ORGANIZATION AND PRODUCTION OF TEST SCENARIOS

The Secure Data Network System (SDNS) [5] program began in August of 1986 through the sponsorship of the National Security Agency (NSA). The goal of the program is to establish a communications architecture and protocols for protecting both unclassified and classified computer networks, within an internationally recognized framework. Security Protocol 4 (SP4) [3,4] is one element of the SDNS, designed to provide security services at layer 4, the Transport layer, of the International Organization for Standardization (ISO)
reference model for Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) [1].

The SP4 standard builds upon the services of either the connectionless or connection oriented Transport layer protocol. It should be viewed as an extension to those protocol standards, rather than as an independent layer protocol. In the OSI architecture, the Transport layer has the sole responsibility to provide reliable end-to-end communications between peer end-systems. SP4 services, therefore, nicely complement those provided by Transport protocols. SP4 functionality is situated near the bottom of the Transport layer and consists of a simple encapsulation/decapsulation mechanism that protects Transport protocol data units within a cryptographically secure envelope. SP4 extends the OSI Transport connectionless and connection oriented services to provide or support the following security services defined in the OSI Security Architecture addendum

The SP4 standard identifies other security functions on which it depends. These functions include key management, security management, and cryptography. Key management is needed to establish and maintain keying material used by SP4; security management is needed for event reporting and auditing; and cryptography (i.e., employment of specific cryptographic algorithms) is needed to support Data Integrity, Data Confidentiality, and Authentication services. These functions are normally collocated in
an end-system, with an SP4 entity.

This paper investigates the conformance assessment of an SP4 implementation and the implications of such a procedure. Since SP4 is compliant with the OSI reference model and security architecture, emphasis is placed on the OSI conformance testing methodology [9]. Two other related assessment methods, interoperability assessment and
- 1-security evaluation, are also reviewed. Like conformance assessment, both are concerned with the correctness of an implementation, albeit from different perspectives.

An implicit assumption made throughout this paper is that for an SP4 implementation to be trustworthy, the SP4 layer protocol entity must be part of the Trusted Computing Base (TCB) [15] for a distributed system. Figure 1 illustrates this view of SP4. A TCB refers to the combination of protection mechanisms within a computer system responsible for enforcing a security policy. In a distributed network environment, this is referred to as a Network Trusted Computing Base (NTCB) [13].

The OSI Transport Layer Security Protocol (TLSP) [6] is a current ISO standard that provides security services similar to SP4. Since SP4 formed the foundation for TLSP, the two specifications are closely related. Therefore, most of the comments and
conclusions in this paper apply equally to TLSP.

Conformance assessment of OSI protocols is defined in a multi-part standard [9] that provides the basic framework and methodology for conformance testing. The scope of the standard ranges from abstract test suite specification and executable test derivation to the conformance assessment process, and includes test methods and a formal notation for describing test cases. The assessment procedure has two distinct parts: a static conformance review of the Protocol Implementation Conformance Statement (PICS) and
dynamic conformance testing of the implementation.

The PICS defines, in a tabular form, the range of functionality (i.e., capabilities and options) afforded by an implementation. Product manufacturers are expected to provide PICS for their implementations according to the PICS proforma established by standardization groups for an OSI protocol. By reviewing the PICS, a determination can be made of whether or not the functionality provided by a product meets the conformance requirements. The PICS also can be used as a guide for selecting appropriate test cases against which to assess the conformance claims of an implementation. The methodology also requires a Protocol Implementation Extra Information for Testing (PIXIT) to identify additional information about an implementation to facilitate testing, such as address values,

Conformance testing for OSI is the process of verifying that the external behavior of an implemented data communications protocol agrees with the requirements specified in the defining standard. The OSI conformance testing methodology relies on a black box testing approach. That is, the internals of the box, or in this situation the protocol implementation under test, are unexaminable and unknown. How the protocol functionality is implemented is not part of the methodology. Instead, emphasis is placed

The external behavior of an OSI protocol implementation is observable through the protocol data units (PDUs) exchanged with a test system, and is the foundation for the design of test scenarios. OSI conformance test scenarios contain negative as well as positive tests. That is, test scenarios include test cases involving the use of invalid PDUs and otherwise inappropriate PDU behavior. Conformance testing can determine whether
are correctly exchanged, services are correctly provided, options are correctly
treated, errors are correctly handled, and events are correctly reported.

While conformance testing increases the probability that different implementations of a set of selected protocols will interwork properly, it is no guarantee of full interoperability, given the typically large number of protocol options and unconstrained
parameters. Supplementary interoperability assessment is also required.

Similar to conformance assessment, the focus of interoperability assessment is testing. Interoperability testing is concerned with the end-to-end operation of one or more OSI implementations, exercising all services with various semantic values, and checking rendition and expected behavior. For example, in the case of messaging systems, the data content must be correctly relayed across several end-systems and correctly rendered to the recipients. Moreover, the distribution and handling within the end-system must behave as

Although interoperability testing also uses a black box approach, it contrasts from conformance testing in several ways. Perhaps the most striking is the change from a test environment involving a validated test system and instrumented implementation, to an operational environment involving many different implementations as counterparts to the testing. Another significant difference is that the OSI conformance testing methodology is concerned primarily with evaluating a single layer or small group of layers, while interoperability testing involves the entire seven layer stack or, in the case of intermediate systems, the lower-level three-layer stack. Interoperability testing also emphasizes positive
as opposed to negative testing, in contrast to conformance testing.

Interoperability testing alone is not a substitute for conformance testing. There always exists the danger of obtaining implementations that are interoperable with each other, but not necessarily conformant to the protocol standard. Because of the emphasis on positive testing, there is also the possibility that interoperability tests would not uncover some types of errors. Therefore, both types of testing are needed to preclude isolated
islands of interoperable but non-conformant implementations.

At present, interoperability testing is not the subject of international standardization, due to a lack of broad consensus of a methodology and framework. Most interoperability testing is conducted on an ad hoc basis, to meet the demands of a particular situation. Implementations intended for a specific management domain may be subjected to interoperability tests as part of the requirement for membership. Many commercial implementations go through such a phase prior to and during vendor demonstrations at international trade shows and conferences. As demonstration software matures into
products, reasonable product interoperability becomes the norm.

security evaluation assesses products to determine the degree of trust that can be placed in them with regard to the secure processing of information. An evaluation is done without regard to the specific operational conditions and circumstances in which a product may be used (e.g., inside a shielded vault), but does take into consideration the

-4-computer system operating environment. The objective of the security evaluation is to perform a technical assessment of the trust properties. Three general security issues that must be addressed are: the confidentiality of the data, the integrity of the data and the system, and the availability of service. The goal or main requirement is to assure that the system behaves according to an organization’s security requirements that, in turn, reflect the defined security policy of the organization. To guarantee that this requirement is met, the security functionality of an implementation must work correctly and effectively.

Evaluations of commercial products in the U.S. are carried out through the Department of Defense (DoD) Trusted Product Evaluation Program (TPEP). The TPEP evaluates systems that meet the DoD’s program objectives based on the criteria defined in the DoD TCSEC [7]. The TCSEC defines a hierarchy of classes that represent increasing levels of confidence in the trustworthiness of a computer system to protect information. The TCSEC identifies features to be evaluated, such as login, access controls, and audit; and assurances to be obtained, such as least privilege, testing, and documentation. Features are mechanisms that provide security functionality, while assurances indicate the degree of trust, and give a measure of the degree to which features

In contrast to conformance and interoperability evaluation techniques, security evaluations are limited to only the security relevant portions of the system. However, an evaluation at higher levels of assurance may be extensive, especially if one considers the attention given such areas as covert channels. Furthermore, testing is only one aspect of a security evaluation. Other aspects include ensuring that the product is produced and distributed according to appropriate controls and standards, and ensuring that well documented procedures exist for the operational use of the product. The goal of an evaluator is to gain a deep understanding of a product and how it meets stated security
objectives, not merely to determine whether it passes a set of predefined tests.

TCSEC evaluations are normally carried out in parallel with product development. Features (i.e., security mechanisms) not only must be operable and correct, but also must be implemented to resist tampering and leakage. From a testing perspective, assurance is gained through testing the implementation’s security functionality and susceptibility to penetration. An evaluator has access to internal documentation and is involved in the product development cycle. Security evaluations under the TCSEC can be considered a form of white box testing, since the internals of the box can be observed and controlled, and specifications of the internal design are available for analysis. White box testing is typically more stringent than black box testing since it allows test case design to establish some measure of minimum execution coverage with respect to the structural properties of
Several characteristics of the SP4 standard are important to note, since they have
an effect on the various forms of assessment. They are:

Although concerned with the provision of security services through specific types of security mechanisms, the SP4 standard does not contain any requirements on the level of confidence in the security provided by an implementation of the protocol. That is, the SP4 standard is a functionality specification devoid of assurance requirements for the implementation and the operating environment. Therefore, an implementation may fully conform to the SP4 standard, yet be inherently insecure. For example, there are no guarantees that a system correctly implementing SP4 either employs algorithms with an appropriate strength of mechanism, or controls access to transmitted information once it resides in the system. The level of assurance provided by an SP4 implementation depends on factors outside the scope of the standard. That assurance can be gained only by
evaluating the implementation according to an established set of criteria, such as the Trusted Computer System Evaluation Criteria (TCSEC) or Trusted Network

The SP4 standard is mechanism dependent, but algorithm independent. For example, the Data Confidentiality service is provided through an encipherment mechanism, but the underlying cryptographic algorithm is left open in the specification. Furthermore, an SP4 implementation may legitimately support only a subset of the optional elements indicated in the standard. To compensate for the openness and flexibility in the standard, implementors’ groups are expected to develop security sub-profiles for generic applications. That is, the characteristics of the required security functionality must be stipulated before

security sub-profile specifies the general security objectives and operating environment assumptions, a target range of assurance, and suites of protection algorithms, in addition to the set of security features selected from those offered by the protocol. Therefore, a protection profile not only tightens the functionality specification, but also supplements it with assurance requirements. Few examples of security sub-profiles exist. Probably the best known example is that done for Message Handling Systems based on the

-6-In practice, a fully capable SP4 implementation is an implementation of a Transport protocol with embedded SP4 functionality. Because of the dependency on the Transport protocol, conformance testing of SP4 implementations is expected to be tied closely to Transport layer conformance testing procedures. The next chapter discusses this in more detail. The implication of the dependency for a security evaluation is that both the SP4
and Transport layer protocol implementations would require evaluation.

Clearly, the objective and scope of the three categories of assessment are quite different. Conformance assessment is the most functionally precise, since it provides testing at the level of detail of the functional standard, on a protocol-by-protocol basis. Interoperability assessment is a bit broader since it concerns a group of layer protocols and their operational aspects, and seeks functional compatibility among many implementations. Security evaluation is somewhat orthogonal to both. In the case of SP4, it is broader in scope than conformance testing of a protocol entity, yet narrower than interoperability testing of an entire end-system. The target of a security evaluation, the trusted computing base, lies somewhere in between. Similarly, while the objective of a security evaluation goes beyond functionality and seeks adherence to assurance requirements, only the correctness and effectiveness of the implementation from a security perspective are of concern. Therefore, it is possible to successfully evaluate an SP4 implementation that lacks conformance to the standard and does not interoperate with

Although OSI conformance testing does not directly address trust-related factors of an implementation, a successful conformance testing result suggests a level of assurance for the implementation. That result could be provided to a security evaluation to satisfy some portion of the functional testing requirements of the TCB. Since systems may be exploited through an external interface such as that provided by OSI, consideration could be given to incorporate extended functionality testing based on design information, and penetration testing with the conformance testing methodology. That is, contrary to the traditional view of separate conformance and security evaluations, conformance testing could be integrated into the security evaluation process and be made a part of the evaluation procedure for a distributed system that relies on a lower layer security protocol

One interesting difference between conformance and security evaluations is in the structure of the processes and the roles that the organizations play in them. The security evaluation of a product is normally done through a sponsoring governmental agency, includes product development as part of the process, is conducted at a secure government facility using procedures not completely disclosed to the public, and continues until the
criteria level is met or the developer gives up. conformance evaluation on the other

-7-hand is normally initiated by the developer, is conducted after product development, is evaluated at a government accredited facility through publicly available test procedures, and renders a pass/fail verdict within a comparatively short period of time. Whereas the security evaluation process is centered around the concerns of the evaluation agency, the conformance evaluation process is oriented more toward the developer. In particular, the black box nature of conformance testing avoids disclosure of proprietary information by the developer.

Interoperability testing appears to logically fall after successful conformance and security evaluations take place. Ideally, a rigorous conformance testing campaign would limit the effort needed for interoperability testing, making it merely an exercise in system configuration and parameter determination. In this respect, interoperability testing is
complimentary to both conformance testing and security evaluation.

This section applies the OSI Conformance Testing Methodology and Framework to SP4 and develops a consistent approach for conformance testing of an implementation, to meet the dynamic conformance conditions. The procedure is predicated on the following
(a) Communication hardware/software products for OSI will provide an exposed interface (i.e., an external interface to the user) from the Transport layer
(b) Implementations of the SP4 protocol are not guaranteed to provide an exposed interface, and are most likely embedded within the Transport
(c) Based on its functionality, SP4 may be considered as the lowest sub-layer of

The implication of these assumptions is that an SP4 implementation must be tested indirectly, through the interface to the Transport protocol entity. The approach taken is to build upon extant testing requirements for the Government Open System Interconnection Profile (GOSIP) [12]. The abstract test method proposed for SP4 follows a coordinated single-layer embedded test method. This approach assumes that explicit test coordination procedures can be used with the Transport implementation containing and/or supporting SP4 functionality. Figure 2 illustrates this test method for SP4. The system under test must involve a Transport implementation whose normal non-security services have been successfully tested. Here the Transport protocol interface is used as the point of control and observation (PCO) for the upper tester, in lieu of an exposed SP4 interface. SP4 behavior is exercised and analyzed indirectly through the Transport interface. The
PCO for the lower tester is the underlying Network service interface.

For the coordinated test method, the upper tester for the SP4 implementation under test (lUT) contains a test responder capable of processing a test management protocol (TMP) and performing the indicated actions on the lUT. The composition of the lower tester is a bit more complex. It must be capable of realizing Transport services by processing executable test scenarios, while maintaining a correspondence with the peer test responder of the upper tester. In addition, the lower tester can normally manipulate Transport PDU (TPDU) encodings for exception generation, and record messages concerning the progress of the test scenario and the detailed TPDU exchanges. From the
latter information, a verdict analysis can be performed.
Other concerns about SP4 conformance testing that are related to security, include
(a) Determination of the default cryptographic algorithms for testing,
(b) Key management support for establishing and maintaining traffic encryption
(c) The control and selection of security services, and
(d) The method for collecting security event reports.
These and other such items should be addressed in the PIXIT supplied with the SP4 implementation to be tested.

The coordinated single-layer embedded (CSE) test method requires that the Transport protocol be tested as a prerequisite to testing the SP4 functionality. Similarly, the cryptographic facility that supports the protocol entity should complete successful independent testing to avoid confounding the conformance test results. Standard algorithm test suites would be useful in testing the cryptographic facility and for simplifying

-10-Unlike other protocols, lower layer security protocols have the unique property of silence in situations where a security violation occurs. That is, rather than responding to the source of the offending PDU, a security event is reported and the offending PDU is discarded. This type of behavior complicates verdict determination, since the verdict is dependent on the security event reporting function for the system under test. Realization of the CSE test method, therefore, may require shifting some of the responsibility for
verdict determination onto the upper tester.
3.3 Characteristics of the Means of Testing

The realization of an abstract test method includes the test system, executable test suite, testing support tools, and documentation. The following items, drawn from the GOSIP conformance testing technical criteria [12], summarize the significant characteristics
of the means of testing needed for the coordinated test method proposed:
(a) Capability to analyze PICS and PIXIT for the lUT and to select and parameterize tests to be run, and to configure the means of testing for
communication with the System Under Test (SUT);
(b) Procedures to reconcile and test data with the test purposes and yield
a verdict for each test purpose;
(c) Capability to produce Conformance Test Reports, listing test cases executed and their verdicts, and detailing the lUT behavior in cases of failure;
(d) Capability to record the protocol data units exchanged with the lUT in a conformance log, and to review the structure and encoding of protocol data
units after the test campaign is complete;
(e) Capability to assemble SE TPDUs according to the SP4 standard, and send them to an end-system under test over any supported medium;
(f) Capability to receive and disassemble SE TPDUs according to the SP4 standard, to validate the SE TPDUs received, and to record the results;
(g) Capability to construct invalid as well as valid SE TPDUs;
(h) Capability to monitor and to initiate SE TPDU exchanges with the SUT, and
(i) Capability to control and coordinate the SUT, in order to induce the SUT to generate specified types of SE TPDUs, including control and coordination
with the Transport entity associated with the SP4 lUT,
ORGANIZATION AND PRODUCTION OF TEST SCENARIOS

Within the U.S. Federal Government, the Government OSI Profile (GOSIP) [11] is the procurement specification for agencies to use when acquiring open systems computer network products. GOSIP conformance testing procedures [12] have been established that follow the OSI conformance testing methodology. At the Transport layer, GOSIP mandates class 4 Transport for interoperability among compliant systems. The remaining classes have a less essential role in the specification, as does the connectionless Transport protocol. For this reason, and because class 4 functionality encompasses that of the other
classes, only class 4 test cases are considered in the discussion that follows.

The abstract test cases for the class 4 Transport protocol fall into one of three categories of increasing complexity and functionality: basic interconnection tests, capability tests, and behavior tests. Basic interconnection tests establish a baseline capability and determine the ability of the implementation to open and close connections, and convey normal user data, and parameters. Capability tests continue to examine fully all mandatory capabilities and determine whether the implementation can convey expedited data, and more extensive amounts of normal user data. Behavior tests establish the extent to which the dynamic conformance requirements are met and examine the ability of the implementation to negotiate parameters, to be involved in more complicated exchanges,
and to handle the full range of error conditions.

GOSIP test scenarios for class 4 Transport are not capable of providing insight into an SP4 lUT, other than to establish that fundamental communications capabilities are in good order. Furthermore, the behavior tests are no longer appropriate since they do not address the specific services offered by SP4. These security services are embodied in the security encapsulation (SE) TPDU, used exclusively by the SP4 protocol. None of the error conditions associated with the SE TPDU are part of the existing behavior tests.
The SP4 PICS proforma [8] suggests areas that should be included in the test suite coverage. Note that some areas may overlap with others since they may be merely
different views of the same functionality. Tests should exist for the following areas:
- ability to generate valid SE - ability to handle SE TPDUs in TPDUs
- ability to accept valid SE - ability to handle network failure TPDUs
- explicit security labeling - final sequence number checking
- invalid key identifier - invalid integrity check value
- invalid peer address - invalid final sequence number
The test coverage areas give guidelines for test case development that need to be further specified and organized into test categories. The details of test specifications are
left to the designer of abstract test scenarios for SP4.

original_blocks.html: For the coordinated test method, the upper tester for the SP4 implementation under test (IUT) contains a test responder capable of processing a test management protocol (TMP) and performing the indicated actions on the IUT. The composition of the lower tester is a bit more complex. It must be capable of realizing Transport services by processing executable test scenarios, while maintaining a correspondence with the peer test responder of the upper tester. In addition, the lower tester can normally manipulate Transport PDU (TPDU) encodings for exception generation, and record messages concerning the progress of the test scenario and the detailed TPDU exchanges. From the latter information, a verdict analysis can be performed.
